newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian region votes "no" to nuclear plant.
newsitem.headline: Russian region votes "no" to nuclear plant.

text.p: People in central Russia's Kostroma region, dotted with crystal-clear lakes, have rejected a plan to build a nuclear power plant in the country's first such referendum, officials said on Monday.

"We are very pleased," said Karen Richardson, an anti-nuclear campaigner from the Greenpeace environmental organisation. "People were given the choice for the first time and they showed they do not want to spoil their region's ecology."
Many Russians, including Muscovites, have holiday homes in Kostroma -- about 200 km (125 miles) northeast of the capital and renowned for pure air and the clean water in its rivers and lakes.
Preliminary results showed 87 percent of those voting were against the plant and only 10 percent in favour. Turnout was 59 percent.
In Soviet days the Kremlin took the decisions on where to build nuclear power plants, chemical factories or waste dumps, issuing orders to local administrations to comply.

Most new nuclear projects in Russia have been delayed since the April 1986 Chernobyl disaster, the world's worst nuclear accident, when a reactor at the Ukrainian power plant exploded and sent clouds of radiation across Europe.
Campaigners for the Kostroma plant tried to tempt voters by saying the nuclear station would create jobs and improve the region's economy, Richardson said.
"But people are bearing in mind what may happen if something goes wrong. They remember that it is the 10th anniversary of the Chernobyl disaster," she added.

However, RIA news agency quoted a local official as saying last week there had never been any firm plans to build the station and that the referendum was only part of a campaign for votes in an election of the local governor.
Nuclear power already accounts for 12 percent of the electricity generated in Russia, and safety issues are acute for many people living across the 150-million state.

Minor malfunctions stopped reactors at two Russian nuclear power plants and another one was on the brink of a shut-down due to a strike last week, but industry officials said none of the cases was dangerous or involved radiation leakage.
Employees at St Petersburg's nuclear power plant, where some workers downed tools on Thursday to demand wage arrears be paid, suspended the strike over the weekend.
Officials said they had been ready to shut the reactors if the strike provoked a smallest danger to the plant's safety.
